title: Release guard and registry credentials still sit only in workflow code that the triggering tag or branch supplies
description: Unchanged since run 2: `git log 4f9c7103..7ae1808 -- .github/workflows/release.yml .github/workflows/tag.yml` lists no commit. release.yml runs on any pushed tag matching v* (lines 9-12). On a push event GitHub runs the workflow file stored at the pushed commit, so both the guard job (lines 24-58: tagged commit must be an ancestor of origin/main, newest ci.yml run for the SHA must be green) and the release job come from a file the tag author chooses. The release job's only link to the guard is `needs: guard` (line 61). It binds no `environment:`, and no workflow under .github/workflows declares one. DOCKERHUB_USERNAME/DOCKERHUB_TOKEN (lines 118-119) and HARBOR_USERNAME/HARBOR_PASSWORD (lines 125-126) are therefore repository or organization secrets. GitHub hands those to any non-fork workflow run on any ref. A principal who can push a v* tag can point it at a commit whose release.yml drops the guard, then build and push noixdev/pulsix-manager and noixdev/pulsix-worker under the version tag and `latest` to Docker Hub and harbor.cloud.noidee.dev. The compose stack defaults every Pulsix image to `latest`: the x-manager-base anchor shared by manager and cli (deploy/compose/docker-compose.yml:15), worker-enroll (line 158) and worker (line 191). An installation that keeps the default would pull such an image into the manager, which holds the master key and DB URL, and into the worker. tag.yml (workflow_dispatch only at line 37, `contents: write` at line 46, `secrets: inherit` at line 61) can be dispatched from any branch carrying an edited copy, and the commit pin at line 60 binds only the copy that runs. Neither route adds a principal beyond 'can push a ref': any pushed branch workflow can name repository secrets directly. The guard is therefore not a security boundary against write users, only against mistakes. A secondary weakness applies even when a genuine main release.yml runs. Its CI query (lines 52-54) takes the newest ci.yml run for head_sha with no event or branch filter, and ci.yml also runs on pull_request (ci.yml:2). A pull_request run whose workflow definition comes from a writer-controlled base branch can therefore satisfy the guard for a main commit whose CI failed. Exploitability depends entirely on hosted facts. Local history has one author, noidee (all 1013 commits). Backlog 1.38 records five automatic tag.yml runs (Actions has run in this repository at some point), while backlog 7.17 says CI is disabled. Backlog 7.16 still lists 'registry secrets belong in a protected release environment' as open.
claimed_root_cause: Release authorization is enforced only in workflow code that the triggering ref supplies: the guard job in release.yml, and tag.yml when it is dispatched from a branch. The registry push credentials are repository or organization secrets, not environment secrets behind a tag-only deployment rule or required reviewers. Any principal who can push a ref (a v* tag, or any branch carrying a workflow) can therefore reach them, and nothing outside attacker-editable YAML separates that principal from a release-authorized one. The guard's CI query also accepts a ci.yml run of any event type for the SHA.

trace.description: Any pushed tag matching v* starts the workflow. For push events GitHub runs the workflow definition stored at the tagged commit (GITHUB_SHA), so the tag author chooses which release.yml runs, including one without the guard job.

The on-main check (merge-base --is-ancestor, lines 34-42) and the CI-green check (lines 44-58) live in that same tag-supplied file. The CI query at line 53 filters only on workflow file and head_sha, with no event=push or branch=main filter.

The publish job's only gate is `needs: guard` in the same file. No `environment:` key is bound, so GitHub evaluates no deployment protection rule (tag pattern, reviewers) before giving the job secrets.

trace.scope: on.workflow_dispatch; permissions contents: write (line 46); jobs.tag secrets: inherit (line 61)
trace.description: workflow_dispatch runs the tag.yml copy on whichever branch the dispatcher selects, with contents: write and every repository secret. The commit pin at line 60 protects only the copy that is dispatched. This is the same principal class as a tag pusher, not a new one.

trace.scope: jobs.release: Docker Hub/Harbor login (lines 115-126) and build-push (lines 128-156)
trace.description: secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN (line 119) and secrets.HARBOR_PASSWORD (line 126) are handed to a job with no environment. build-push-action then pushes the version tag and `latest` of pulsix-manager and pulsix-worker to Docker Hub and harbor.cloud.noidee.dev.

evidence.description: The comment states the intended invariant: a tag is not evidence, a hand-pushed tag must not be trusted, and the thing that publishes does the checking. The check lives in the tag-supplied file, so it cannot hold against the tag pusher.
The safety argument covers fork pull requests only. It assumes any write user who creates a tag is fine, which is the assumption the guard was meant to drop.
The CI query `workflows/ci.yml/runs?head_sha=$SHA&per_page=1` has no event or branch filter.
ci.yml triggers on [push, pull_request]. A pull_request run reports the PR head as head_sha but takes its workflow definition from the merge ref, so it can satisfy the guard's query.
`secrets: inherit` remains, together with workflow_dispatch (line 37) and contents: write (line 46).

The x-manager-base anchor (manager and cli) uses noixdev/pulsix-manager:${PULSIX_VERSION:-latest}. worker-enroll (line 158) and worker (line 191) default to latest too, so a pushed `latest` reaches installations that keep the default.
Backlog 7.16 lists 'the registry secrets belong in a protected release environment (1.38)' as still open outside this repo, which confirms they are not environment-bound today.

Backlog 1.38 records five failed automatic tag.yml runs, so Actions has executed in this repository at some point. Backlog 7.17 (line 560) says CI is disabled, so whether Actions is enabled now is an open hosted fact.

blockers: Hosted fact: the scope of DOCKERHUB_USERNAME, DOCKERHUB_TOKEN, HARBOR_USERNAME and HARBOR_PASSWORD. Each is a repository secret or an organization secret, and for an organization secret the repository access list matters. Source shows only that they are not environment secrets: no `environment:` key exists in any workflow.

Hosted fact: whether any principal can push a branch or a v* tag, or dispatch workflows, without being authorized to cut releases. That means collaborators, teams, and GitHub Apps or bots with write or maintain access, plus any ruleset restricting refs/tags/v* creation. Local history has a single author (1013 commits by noidee). If every writer is a release manager, the bypass is same-principal and not a vulnerability.
Hosted fact: whether GitHub Actions is currently enabled for NoiXdev/pulsix (backlog 1.38 and 7.17 conflict), and whether any installation consumes the published `latest` images.
No safe local check: demonstrating secret release to a guardless tag-supplied workflow needs a real GitHub Actions run, and this audit may not contact GitHub or publish anything.

validation_plan.local: No in-audit local reproduction exists, because GitHub Actions secret delivery cannot be emulated offline. Source checks already done: release.yml and tag.yml are unchanged since 4f9c7103; no workflow declares `environment:`; the guard query has no event or branch filter. Optional owner-run step, outside this audit, never against NoiXdev/pulsix or a real registry: in a throwaway personal repository with a dummy repository secret REG_TOKEN=marker, (a) commit on main a release.yml with a guard job (fail unless the commit is on main) and a release job that prints only the length or sha256 of REG_TOKEN. Commit a guardless copy on a side branch, push tag v0.0.0-test at that commit, and observe the release job reading the secret. (b) Move REG_TOKEN into an environment `release` whose deployment rule allows only v* tags, with a tag ruleset restricting creation to a maintainer, and add `environment: release`. Repeat and observe that the secret is withheld or the job waits for review.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed only. Push no tag and no image. (1) In NoiXdev/pulsix Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions, and in the NoiXdev organization equivalent, record whether the four registry secrets are repository or organization secrets. For organization secrets, record which repositories can use them. (2) In Settings > Collaborators and teams and in the installed GitHub Apps, list every principal with write or maintain access. In Settings > Rules, check whether any ruleset restricts creating refs/tags/v* and who may bypass it. (3) Confirm whether Actions is enabled for the repository. The finding holds if the secrets are repository- or organization-scoped and any write principal or app is not meant to release. Fix: create a `release` environment whose deployment rule allows only v* tags (backed by a tag ruleset), optionally with a required reviewer. Move the four registry secrets into it and add `environment: release` to jobs.release. Add `&event=push&branch=main` to the guard's CI query. Replace tag.yml's `secrets: inherit` with the single declared secret once the shared workflow declares it (backlog 7.16 follow-up).

title: A mount point with a quote and a non-UTF-8 byte still poisons the agent's stream after the 7.40 fix
description: The 7.40 fix makes the disk plugin skip mount points the manager would refuse because they are too long or contain control characters. It does not skip mount points that are not valid UTF-8. gopsutil v4.26.8 runs each /proc/1/mountinfo path through unescapeFstab, which is strconv.Unquote. A path that contains a double quote fails to unquote and comes back as its raw bytes, so a byte such as 0xFF survives. Without the quote the byte is normalised to U+FFFD and is harmless. The item field of CheckResult is a proto3 string, so grpc-go refuses to encode the message on the client side and finishes the whole client stream. handleResults puts the unsent results back into the disconnect buffer. On every reconnect, streamSession sends facts and then calls activateSender, which replays the buffer before the first heartbeat. The replay fails on the same chunk and the session ends. The disk tick adds the item again at every interval, so the poison never ages out of the 15-minute buffer. The effect: a local user who can mount something in PID 1's mount namespace on a directory named, for example, a"\xffb stops that host's check results, heartbeats and configuration convergence. Facts still arrive at each stream open, and each open touches last_seen, so the host does not look offline. Its rule tuples go to unknown ('no data') after three check intervals, and no threshold alert can fire on it. Production placement does not change this. The shipped unit has ProtectHome=true and PrivateTmp=true, so statfs on a mount under /home or /tmp fails inside the agent's namespace. The plugin then emits three error observations that carry the same invalid item (disk.go:141-145) instead of value observations. The poison is the same either way.
root_cause: reportableItem (internal/agent/checks/disk.go:37-41) mirrors only the manager's length and control-character rules. It leaves out the wire contract's UTF-8 requirement for proto3 string fields, even though gopsutil can return raw non-UTF-8 bytes for a mount point that contains a double quote. The session layer also treats a client-side encode failure like a transport failure. handleResults (session.go:366-385) and activateSender (session.go:321-344) put the unencodable chunk back and replay it ahead of every heartbeat, with no end.
intended_behavior: Any mount point that cannot be carried on the wire is left out, like an over-long one. A chunk the client cannot encode is dropped or quarantined instead of replayed, so one item can never stop the host's other check results, heartbeats or configuration convergence.

trace.description: Discovery mode (no 'mounts' param) reads every mount point through gopsutil Partitions(ctx, true), which parses /proc/1/mountinfo. A local user who can mount (FUSE via setuid fusermount) chooses the path. unescapeFstab (gopsutil disk_unix.go:57-63) returns the raw bytes when strconv.Unquote fails on an embedded '"'.
The only filter is reportableItem, which checks the length and control, U+2028 and U+2029 runes. Invalid UTF-8 decodes to U+FFFD, which is not a control rune, so the item passes.

Three value observations carry the mount point unchanged as Item. When statfs fails, for example under the unit's ProtectHome or PrivateTmp, lines 141-145 emit three error observations with the same Item instead.
Item is copied into the Result batch handed to the session sink (Loop.handleResults).

The results become a CheckResults message, and stream.Send (session.go:62) encodes it. Marshalling fails with 'string field contains invalid UTF-8', grpc-go returns codes.Internal and finishes the client stream, and later Sends return EOF.
The unsent results, including the poisoned item, go back into the disconnect buffer. While no sender is live, every disk tick adds them there too.

Every reconnect replays the buffer before the first heartbeat (session.go:185-201). The replay fails on the poisoned chunk, pending[sent:] goes back at session.go:336, and streamSession returns an error. loop.go:270-279 reconnects with jittered backoff indefinitely, so no heartbeat or check result is ever delivered.

evidence.description: reportableItem checks len(item) and unicode.IsControl/U+2028/U+2029 only. There is no utf8.ValidString.
'string item = 2;' in a file declared syntax = "proto3" (line 1). google.golang.org/protobuf refuses to marshal invalid UTF-8 in it.
A failed replay puts pending[sent:] back into the buffer and returns an error. That happens before the heartbeat at session.go:201.
A failed session is retried with jittered backoff, with no limit on attempts.
The manager treats each stream open as a heartbeat (Touch), so last_seen keeps moving while no real heartbeat or result arrives.

ProtectHome=true (with PrivateTmp=true on line 30) makes statfs on user-owned mounts fail inside the agent's namespace. The mount is still read from /proc/1/mountinfo and is emitted as error observations with the same invalid item, so the hardening does not block the path.

conditions.description: A local unprivileged account on a monitored host.

The account can create a mount in PID 1's mount namespace, for example FUSE through setuid fusermount/fusermount3, on a directory it controls whose name contains '"' and a non-UTF-8 byte. The 7.40 fix comment and backlog row name this capability as the threat model the fix defends against. Whether a given distribution allows it is a deployment fact.
The disk check runs in discovery mode, with no explicit 'mounts' list. This is the default. Explicit mounts arrive as JSON strings from the manager and are valid UTF-8.

execution.attacker_perspective: An unprivileged local user on a host running the Pulsix agent, who can mount a FUSE filesystem on a directory they own.
payloads: mountinfo line: 40 22 0:50 / /home/u/q"\xffz rw,nosuid,nodev,relatime shared:30 - fuse.sshfs u@h:/ rw,user_id=1000,group_id=1000
instructions: Copy the repository to scratch. Add internal/agent/checks/v02_poison_test.go, which writes a fixture mountinfo with a '/' ext4 line, the payload line and a control line /home/u/n\xffz that has no quote. It sets HOST_PROC_MOUNTINFO to the fixture, calls diskPlugin{gopsutilPartitions{}, fakeUsage}.Collect, logs each item's utf8.ValidString and reportableItem result, and proto.Marshals the resulting CheckResults.

Add internal/agent/v02_replay_test.go. It starts an in-memory bufconn gRPC AgentService that acks every message and counts stream opens, heartbeats and results. It builds a real Loop with NewLoop and puts the poisoned result plus a good result into the buffer through handleResults. Then, three times: it opens a real client AgentStream, calls activateSender, sends a heartbeat on the same sender, calls Recv, deactivates the sender, and re-adds the poison as a disconnected disk tick would. A control Loop without the poison runs the same steps.

Run each test in the approved Docker sandbox (--network none, read-only, env -i, resource limits): go test -count=1 -v -run TestV02DiscoveredMountItems ./internal/agent/checks/ and go test -count=1 -v -run TestV02PoisonReplayBlocksEveryReconnect ./internal/agent/.
execution.observed_result: Collect returned 9 observations with no error. The item '/home/u/q"\xffz' had validUTF8=false and reportable=true. The control item without a quote was normalised to '/home/u/n\uFFFDz' and was valid. proto.Marshal failed with 'string field contains invalid UTF-8'. In the replay harness, each of 3 reconnects failed the same way. activateSender returned 'replay buffered check results: rpc error: code = Internal desc = grpc: error while marshaling: string field contains invalid UTF-8', the following heartbeat Send returned EOF, and Recv returned the same Internal error. The live sender was never installed, and the buffered count grew 2, 3, 4. The server recorded 3 stream opens, 0 heartbeats and 0 check results. The control loop replayed and sent its heartbeat without error.

remediation.strategy: Add utf8.ValidString to reportableItem, which covers both discovered and explicit mounts. Add the same check to the manager's withinContract for parity. Update the plugin's error text and the 7.40 test to cover the UTF-8 rule. Defence in depth in the session: treat a client-side encode failure (codes.Internal 'error while marshaling' returned by Send before anything reaches the wire) as a poison chunk to drop and log rather than re-buffer, so no single result can block heartbeats. Add a regression test with a mountinfo fixture that contains '"' plus 0xFF, expects the mount to be skipped, and expects every Collect output to marshal.

likelihood.reason: It needs a local account on a monitored host plus the ability to mount in init's namespace, for example FUSE with setuid fusermount. Many hosts allow this, but it is a deployment fact. The attacker needs one directory name and one mount, with no ongoing effort.

impact.reason: Monitoring of that one host stops persistently while the mount exists. No check results reach the manager, and no heartbeats are sent, which also stops configuration convergence. Threshold alerts for the host cannot fire. The host still looks seen, because stream opens touch last_seen and facts still arrive. Its rule tuples fall to unknown ('no data'), so the gap shows in the UI but is not reported as the host being offline. Other hosts and tenants are unaffected, and no data is disclosed or modified.

confidence.reason: I reproduced the whole chain independently in the approved sandbox with the real gopsutil v4.26.8 parser, real protobuf marshalling, a real grpc-go client stream and the agent's own Loop.handleResults, activateSender and sendHeartbeat. A control case passed. The reconnect-forever step follows from the loop.go:270-279 source.

title: One host agent can grow hosts.facts without bound, and every org-wide host read pays for it
description: The manager limits a facts push to 64 keys and each value to 512 bytes. It does not limit key length or key characters. Only the 16 MiB gRPC receive limit bounds key length. It also does not limit the number of distinct keys across pushes. The store merges with jsonb ||, which never removes a key. So one host agent identity (root on one compromised host) can loop on its own AgentStream. Each Facts message carries 64 new keys of about 256 KiB, roughly 16 MiB per message. This grows the agent's own hosts.facts until Postgres's jsonb size limit (about 255 MB) refuses the UPDATE. There is no per-stream message rate bound, and each push rewrites the whole growing jsonb value. The inflated document persists. No code path trims facts, so recovery needs operator action outside the product's facts path. ListAllHosts (SELECT * FROM hosts) reads the facts column and json-decodes every host's facts into map[string]any. It runs through checks.Service.ResolveHost/ResolveHosts/ResolveOrg → checksHostRoster.MonitoredHosts: on every heartbeat-driven resolve of every agent in the organization (at most once per 10 s per agent), on every rule evaluation's ContextForHost, on every inventory render, preview and job snapshot, and on several API and template paths. The paginated host list (ListHosts, also SELECT *) returns the document whenever that host is on the page. Inventory render also embeds the document as pulsix_facts when the host is in scope. One host's inflated document is therefore transferred and decoded many times per minute by the shared manager process and database. That load also lands on other tenants on the same instance. Locally observed so far: only the service layer and wire limits accept the input. Database growth and the cost of the reads are not observed.
claimed_root_cause: Service.RecordFacts (internal/agents/facts.go:67-83) mirrors only part of the collector's normalization: the per-push key count and the value byte length. It omits key length, key charset and any aggregate bound on stored keys or document size. UpsertHostFacts (internal/db/queries/agents.sql:119-122) merges with jsonb || and keeps every key ever reported. There is no column CHECK on hosts.facts (internal/db/migrations/00010_hosts.sql:31). Hot org-wide paths read the full row (ListAllHosts SELECT *, internal/db/queries/hosts.sql:102) and decode it (internal/hosts/store_sql.go:246-252).

trace.description: On the mTLS-authenticated AgentStream of one host agent, every Facts message goes to FactsSink.RecordFacts for that agent's own org and host. receiveMessages (stream.go:89-127) has no rate or count bound. The shared gRPC server allows messages up to 16 MiB (internal/grpcsrv/server.go:181, internal/pb/workerpb/limits.go:20).
Checks only len(facts)<=64, non-empty keys and len(value)<=512. Key length and the total across pushes are not checked.
The map is json.Marshal'ed and passed whole to UpsertHostFacts in an org-scoped write transaction.
facts = COALESCE(facts,'{}') || $facts merges the new keys, and keys missing from the push are kept forever. The only ceiling is Postgres's own jsonb size limit.
Every checks ResolveHost/ResolveHosts/ResolveOrg (internal/checks/resolver.go:324,365,409) loads ListAllHosts for the organization, facts column included, only to collect monitored host IDs.

Each host row's facts are json.Unmarshal'ed into map[string]any on every such read: heartbeat resolve, rule-evaluation context, inventory render and job snapshot, and the ListAllHosts API and template paths.

evidence.description: Values are the only thing whose size is checked. Keys have no length limit (constants at facts.go:28-37 define only MaxFactsKeys and MaxFactsValueLen).
The jsonb || merge. The query comment (agents.sql:110-118) says every key the agent did not report survives untouched.
facts jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}' with no size CHECK.
ListAllHosts is SELECT * FROM hosts WHERE org_id = $1, so it includes facts and has no pagination.
Heartbeat-driven ResolveHost runs for every agent in the org, at most once per heartbeatResolveInterval = 10 s (internal/agentapi/registry.go:53). It goes through MonitoredHosts to ListAllHosts.
Every inventory render, including job snapshots, loads ListAllHosts. renderer.go:182 copies Facts into render.Host, and render.go:390-391 emits it as pulsix_facts for in-scope hosts.

MaxRecvMsgSize = MaxWorkerToManagerBytes (16 MiB) also applies to AgentService, which is registered on the same server (server.go:196). It is the only bound on key length. Independent sandboxed check (agents/v03-agent-data/artifacts/evidence.txt): 3 Facts messages of 64 distinct 261,120-byte keys each marshal to 16,712,389 bytes, under the 16,777,216-byte limit. Service.RecordFacts accepted all of them, and 50,135,040 key bytes were forwarded to the store.

blockers: PostgreSQL cannot run in the approved sandbox: testcontainers and internal/db/testdb are forbidden. So nothing below was observed. The growth of hosts.facts across pushes. The per-push rewrite, TOAST and WAL cost. The exact jsonb ceiling at which UPDATE fails. The bytes and decode time ListAllHosts spends per call with one inflated row. Locally observed: only that the wire limit and the service layer accept and forward 64 distinct keys of about 256 KiB per push (agents/v03-agent-data/artifacts/evidence.txt; also agents/h05-agent-data/artifacts/evidence2.txt).

Whether the repeated read and decode measurably degrades the shared manager or database depends on deployment facts outside the repository: the manager container's memory limit, the database's I/O capacity and statement_timeout, and the number of agents and rules per organization.

validation_plan.local: Use internal/db/testdb in a Postgres-capable environment. Create one org with two monitored hosts A and B. Call agents.SQLStore.RecordFacts on host A 4 times, each with 64 distinct keys of 200 KiB and value "v". After each call, query SELECT pg_column_size(facts), octet_length(facts::text) FROM hosts WHERE id = A. Assert that the size grows monotonically to about 50 MB and that hosts.SQLStore.ListAllHosts returns all 256 keys for host A. Then measure one checks.Service.ResolveHost for host B with runtime.MemStats TotalAlloc and wall time, before and after the inflation, and record the difference. Optionally keep pushing until the UPDATE fails, and record the Postgres error and size at that point to establish the ceiling. Dummy data only, no stress loop.
validation_plan.deployment: On an owner-controlled staging instance, give one test host an inflated facts document of about 50 MB, either through the store or with an UPDATE as the schema owner. Leave the org's other agents heartbeating and the rule ticker running for 10 minutes. Record manager RSS and GC CPU, database read and WAL bytes, and heartbeat-resolve latency. Compare them with the same window before the inflation and with the manager container's memory limit. Then remove the test keys with UPDATE hosts SET facts = '{}' and confirm recovery. No production instance, no saturation test.

title: Compose worker snippet writes the live enrollment token into a compose file with default permissions
description: When an org member with workers.write creates a worker enrollment (POST /api/v1/orgs/{org}/worker-enrollments), the API returns the token plus a docker run snippet and a compose snippet (worker_handlers.go:232). Fix b6a8c56 (backlog 7.39) moved the docker run snippet's token out of the docker client's argv and into its environment. The compose snippet was left as it was: it still inlines the live, single-use worker enrollment token (pxw1 format) as a quoted YAML scalar (`PULSIX_ENROLL_TOKEN: "pxw1...."`, worker_snippets.go:53). The backlog row for 7.39 itself says 'The compose snippet still writes the token into the compose file, whose permissions are the operator's', so this residual is known but has not been fixed. The Add worker dialog offers the compose snippet with a copy button (AddWorkerDialog.tsx:86). Its only note is 'Token valid for one hour, single use ... shown only now' (workers.ts:55-56), with nothing about the file's permissions. To use the snippet, the admin saves it to a file on the worker host. That file's mode comes from the admin's umask (commonly 0644) and from where it is saved. The token stays redeemable until the worker first calls Enroll or the one-hour TTL runs out (EnrollmentTTL, enroll.go:23). Enroll is the one worker RPC that needs no client certificate, and it is rate limited only per client address (grpcsrv/enroll.go:21-33). Redemption checks only the secret hash, that the token is unused and that it has not expired (enroll.go:153). It then signs any CSR for the enrollment's org, zone and name (enroll.go:156) and marks the token used in the same transaction. A local account on the worker host can do this if it can read the file, cannot otherwise control docker (not root, not in the docker group) and can reach the manager's worker endpoint. That account can redeem the token first and receive an authenticated org+zone worker certificate. The genuine worker is then refused. The rogue identity can claim that zone's jobs, and the decrypted credentials they carry, until an admin notices the failed worker and revokes it. After redemption, the copy left in the file is inert: the worker ignores the token once a bundle exists (internal/worker/enroll.go:46-47), and the token is single use. Source establishes the code path completely. Whether a lower-trust reader can reach the file depends on where the admin saves it, the file and directory modes, and whether the host has such accounts. None of these is visible in source.
claimed_root_cause: workerSnippets (internal/api/worker_snippets.go:53) renders the pre-redemption secret into the compose YAML as `PULSIX_ENROLL_TOKEN: %q`. Persisting the snippet as a compose file therefore persists the secret in a file whose access control the product neither sets nor advises. The docker run variant was moved to an owner-only channel (worker_snippets.go:31-39, backlog 7.39), but this one was not. The token is also not bound to anything only the intended host holds, so whoever reads it first wins. Possible fixes: render `PULSIX_ENROLL_TOKEN: ${PULSIX_ENROLL_TOKEN}` (compose interpolation from the invoking shell's environment, matching the docker variant), or reference an env_file the dialog tells the admin to create with mode 0600, and add a dialog or doc note on file permissions.

trace.description: An org member with PermWorkersWrite creates a one-time worker enrollment token. The handler gets the token from CreateEnrollment (line 225) and passes it to workerSnippets (line 232), which returns it in compose_snippet.
The compose snippet embeds the full token as a quoted YAML scalar (`PULSIX_ENROLL_TOKEN: %q`). The docker snippet instead takes the value from the client's environment (lines 36 and 39).

The dialog renders the compose snippet with the token inline (lines 53 and 83) and offers a copy button. Its note (workers.ts:55-56) gives no guidance on the permissions of the file the admin saves on the worker host before running docker compose up.

Redemption checks only the secret hash, that the token is unused and that it has not expired. Whoever presents the token first gets a CSR signed for the enrollment's org, zone and worker name (line 156), and the token is marked used in the same transaction. The anonymous gRPC Enroll (grpcsrv/enroll.go:29) reaches this with only a per-address rate limit.

evidence.description: fmt.Sprintf("      PULSIX_ENROLL_TOKEN: %q", token): the literal secret goes into the compose file content.
The backlog 7.39 fix comment covers only docker run ('The token reaches docker run as its environment ... the environment only for the client's own user and root'). The compose variant is unchanged.
Backlog 7.39 is marked done but states 'The compose snippet still writes the token into the compose file, whose permissions are the operator's': the residual is acknowledged and was not fixed.
EnrollmentTTL = time.Hour: a token saved in the file stays redeemable for up to an hour if the worker does not redeem it first.
Enroll is the one worker RPC callable without a client certificate. It is rate limited only per client address (lines 21-33).
The dialog's tokenNote says only 'Token valid for one hour, single use ... shown only now'. It gives no instruction to keep the compose file owner-only.

Once a usable bundle exists, PULSIX_ENROLL_TOKEN is ignored, so the exposure window is from saving the file until the first successful Enroll or the TTL. After that the copy left in the file is inert.

blockers: Where admins save the compose snippet on a worker host, and that file's mode and its parent directories' traversal permissions, are deployment facts. Source does not set them.

Whether supported worker hosts have local accounts that are not root, not in the docker group and not the admin, can read the file and can reach the manager's worker gRPC endpoint is a deployment fact. Without such an account, no trust boundary is crossed.

The real window between saving the file and the container's first Enroll depends on image pull time and on the admin's workflow, and source cannot show it. The approved sandbox cannot create OS accounts or simulate a multi-user host.
